summary: Intro demo of Redwood model catalog, compatibility heuristics, and bench selection workflow tailored for Aurum Works. Covered catalog filters, benchmark templates, kernel/hardware mapping, routing fallbacks, and security considerations (VPC/KMS/SOC2). Agreed to run a 3-model hosted pilot and exchange bench template and sample payloads.
transcript:
[00:00:00] Marta: Hi everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Marta Gomez from Redwood, AE on the account. We have Ethan from SE and, uh, on our side. How's everyone's audio?
[00:00:07] Priya: Audio's good, thanks. I'm Priya, Head of ML at Aurum Works. Hi, Lena and Daniel are with me.
[00:00:12] Daniel: Yep, hi all.
[00:00:15] Ethan: Great, hey team. Quick agenda: show how our model catalog helps pick open models, walk through bench selection, and show the compatibility matrix to map to your infra, then Q&A. We'll leave 10 minutes at the end for next steps.
[00:00:27] Lena: Sounds good.

[00:00:35] Marta: Before we dive, Priya, quick context — what's the primary workload you want to optimize for? Latency-sensitive customer support generation, or high throughput embedding pipelines?
[00:00:45] Priya: Mainly latency-sensitive — realtime summarization in our customer portal. We also have some nightly batches for embeddings but the near-term priority is the portal flow. Latency under 200 ms end-to-end is, like, our target for short prompts.
[00:00:58] Marta: Great, that's helpful. And current stack?
[00:01:02] Daniel: We're on GCP, using a mix of CPU-hosted microservices and some GPU infra for training. We don't currently self-host inference; we've been evaluating vendors. We have compliance needs — SOC 2 type II, and we need to ensure logs and key material stay in our KMS.
[00:01:16] Ethan: Perfect, we'll touch on Redwood Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private later. For today's catalog demo I'll focus on how you select model candidates and pick bench workloads. Forgive the small text — sharing the catalog UI now. (screen share)

[00:01:35] Ethan: Ok, here is the catalog. Top-left filters: model family, parameter size/quantization support, tokenization type, latencies by target hardware, and bench signals like instruction-following score and hallucination rate. You can create a shortlist and export a bench template.
[00:01:50] Priya: That latency column — is that real observed on Redwood-hosted or synthesized?
[00:01:55] Ethan: Good question. It's observed medians from our internal lab — we run models across representative sequence lengths and hardware profiles, then show a distribution. There is a caveat field: "profiled on X sequence distribution". For customer-specific numbers we recommend a short bench run with your payloads.
[00:02:10] Marta: We also auto-suggest models based on your success criteria; you can weight latency vs quality vs cost and the catalog will rank candidates.

[00:02:22] Daniel: What about quantization? We have a limited budget and quantized variants matter for cost.
[00:02:26] Ethan: Yep. In the model details pane you'll see supported quantization profiles — 8-bit, 4-bit, and experimental Q4_0/Q4_1 variants. The compatibility matrix tells you which kernels are available on which GPU microarchitectures. For example, Q4 kernels may map to Ampere+ and Hopper GPUs differently. We also show expected token throughput and effective cost per token at median batch sizes.
[00:02:46] Priya: Sounds helpful. Do you handle mixed-precision kernels automatically or do we need to recompile?
[00:02:51] Ethan: The runtime selects kernels automatically at deploy time, but we expose switches if you want to pin a quantization profile. For private on-prem, we give a validation checklist to ensure your host drivers and CUDA versions are compatible.

[00:03:06] Lena: Can we see the bench template?
[00:03:09] Ethan: Yep I'm loading the default bench spreadsheet (link: shorturl.com/bench-template). The template has three sections: selection criteria, payload samples, and expected SLOs. Selection criteria include prompt length buckets, instruction-adherence tests, and hallucination/regression examples. We recommend at least 50 prompts split across sizes.
[00:03:26] Priya: We can provide the portal's 90th percentile prompt set — that'll be useful.
[00:03:31] Marta: Great. We'll use that to seed the pilot bench.

[00:03:36] Ethan: Now the compatibility matrix — this part is important for mapping to your GCP fleet. Each model row lists kernel compatibility (e.g., custom fused attention kernels), preferred driver versions, and fallback options. If a kernel isn't available on your GPU, the runtime will route to a functionally-compatible variant, which could be a quantized or lower-precision model with a fallback SLO.
[00:03:56] Daniel: How do fallbacks impact latency SLOs? We need deterministic behavior for SLAs.
[00:04:02] Ethan: You can configure routing policies: strict (no fallback — request fails if primary can't serve), best-effort (fallback allowed, logs trace reasons), or hybrid with canary fallbacks for small percents. Redwood provides observability so you can monitor per-token latency and whether a request hit a fallback. We also emit a header so downstream can know it was a fallback.

[00:04:22] Priya: About security — VPC peering, KMS integration, and audit logs are must-haves.
[00:04:28] Marta: Absolutely. For Private deployments we support customer VPC, HSM/KMS integrations (we've done AWS KMS and GCP KMS), and full audit logs forwarded to your SIEM. For Hosted we offer encryption at rest and optional per-tenant KMS bindings. We'll share the SOC 2 report after this call.
[00:04:44] Lena: Nice, can you do SSO? We need SAML
[00:04:47] Marta: Yep, SSO/SAML support in the console + RBAC for route/model-level permissions.

[00:04:54] Ethan: Back to catalog heuristics — one feature I want to demo is the weighted ranking. I set success criteria: latency weight 0.6, quality 0.3, cost 0.1. It ranks three candidates: OpenLlama-13B-q4_0, Redfall-7B-8bit, and MosaicML-mpt-12B. The shortlist shows predicted median latency on your target hardware (we can map to an n1-standard + T4 example or a GCP A100), plus bench quality signals.
[00:05:16] Priya: Redfall? Is that one of your in-house curated models or a third-party?
[00:05:20] Ethan: It's a community model we've verified in our catalog. Some proper names can get munged in transcripts — it's actually Redfall-7B community variant.

[00:05:26] Daniel: If we pick OpenLlama-13B q4_0, what does the end-to-end pipeline look like? We'll want a short fast-path for caching KV between turns.
[00:05:34] Ethan: The runtime supports persistent KV cache per session and prefix caching for common prompts. For your portal flow we recommend enabling prefix cache at the route level; we also use continuous batching to reduce cost but keep SLOs by pinning max-latency thresholds.
[00:05:48] Priya: Ok. Do you have examples of token-level cost breakdowns in the console?
[00:05:52] Marta: Yes, Console shows token-level cost, per-route breakdown, and we provide a token-cost estimator when you choose a model/quantization. You can simulate monthly cost given expected QPS.

[00:06:03] Ethan: Now I'll kick off a quick mock bench run in the host lab to show the process — note this is the internal lab, not your pilot. Loading bench runner and pushing three short prompts. (few seconds pause)
[00:06:18] Ethan: Results: OpenLlama-13B-q4_0 median p50 generation 85 ms on A100 config, Redfall-7B median 48 ms, MPT-12B median 110 ms. Quality signals: instruction-follow score (0-1) — OpenLlama 0.78, Redfall 0.71, MPT 0.82. Hallucination checks: Redfall slightly higher on a specific knowledge prompt.
[00:06:44] Priya: The numbers are interesting — Redfall wins latency but lower instruction-follow. For our portal we care a lot about correctness.
[00:06:51] Ethan: Exactly. That's why the weighted score is useful. Also note cost per 1k tokens differs: quantized 13B may cost less than a 12B non-quantized variant depending on kernel efficiency.

[00:07:04] Daniel: How reproducible are these in our environment? If we want Dedicated, will we see the same medians?
[00:07:09] Ethan: In Dedicated you'll often see better tail latencies because of reserved capacity and predictable warm caches. We typically observe 5–20% tail improvement for reserved pools. For Private on-prem there's additional variance based on interconnect.

[00:07:22] Lena: Let's talk about the model shortlist selection process for the pilot. What do you recommend for Aurum's pilot sample size?
[00:07:28] Marta: We recommend 2–4 models, with 50–200 prompts each across prompt length buckets. For latency SLO testing include synthetic high QPS bursts to see autoscaling behavior.
[00:07:38] Priya: Sounds reasonable. We'd like the pilot to be hosted first to iterate quickly and then consider Dedicated after validating throughput.
[00:07:44] Ethan: Good plan. Hosted pilot lets us run quick bench loops and provide raw artifacts. We can also provide a dedicated pilot quote if you want to reserve capacity.

[00:07:53] Daniel: On integration — do you provide SDKs or OpenAPI? We want an easy way to toggle models via feature flags.
[00:07:58] Marta: We have REST + official SDKs, and the Console supports per-route model pinning. We also expose standard headers for observability and a rollout API so you can toggle model variants behind a feature flag.
[00:08:10] Priya: And how are model version rollouts handled? We need safe canaries.
[00:08:14] Ethan: We support canary rollouts, percentage-based A/B, and automatic fallback policies. E.g., you can send 5% traffic to a new model, watch quality regressions, then ramp. If a regression triggers an alert, we can automatically fallback to the previous variant.

[00:08:27] Lena: A question on data residency — some customer content must never leave EU. How do you guarantee that?
[00:08:33] Marta: For Hosted we have region controls and will keep data in EU regions where available, plus you can use Private to run in your VPC in a GCP EU region. KMS/HSM options also ensure key material stays in-region.

[00:08:44] Ethan: Quick sidebar on kernel mapping — some models have fused attention kernels that are only available on Hopper. Our compatibility matrix will flag that and suggest an equivalent fallback kernel or a different quantization profile that runs on Ampere with slightly higher latency.
[00:08:59] Daniel: Is there a way to see the kernel-level telemetry per request?
[00:09:03] Ethan: Yes, in Console's trace timeline you can see kernel version, GPU id, whether a KV hit occurred, and if batching combined requests. That level of trace is available in Dedicated and Private; Hosted gives you aggregated traces and per-request headers on demand.

[00:09:17] Priya: Can you show a sample routing policy for strict latency SLOs?
[00:09:21] Ethan: Sure — opening routing policy UI. You can set a max-latency threshold, primary model, secondary model, and a hard fail option. You can also configure regional fallbacks and set a budget for fallback percent.
[00:09:36] Marta: Also worth noting: Optimize suggestions will surface quantization profiles and batching settings recommended for your benchmark to hit cost and latency targets.

[00:09:45] Daniel: On compliance logs — can we export to BigQuery or Splunk?
[00:09:49] Marta: Yes we support exporting audit logs to BigQuery, S3, or forward to Splunk. We also provide sampling controls so you can avoid PII leaking into logs; full content logging requires opt-in and special contracts.

[00:10:01] Priya: Ok, a few quick objections — we already have a vendor doing embeddings and a vendor doing hosted chat. What would make Redwood worth consolidating with?
[00:10:11] Marta: Two things: unified inference control across Hosted/Dedicated/Private so you can migrate without changing code, and strong observability plus cost controls. Many teams find it saves them re-architecting for private workloads.
[00:10:24] Ethan: And our model catalog is curated with bench signals and kernel compatibility so you reduce trial-and-error. Instead of spinning up 10 models, you pick 2–3 with high confidence.

[00:10:34] Lena: Are there any limitations around streaming / function calling in open models?
[00:10:38] Ethan: Streaming is supported for most decoder-only models; function-calling is model-dependent. We provide structured-output helpers in the SDK to normalize function-calling across models.

[00:10:48] Marta: Alright, quick demo wrap — I'll summarize and then Ethan will run through what we'll do for the pilot. Summary: we'll share the catalog export and bench template, Aurum will provide the prompt set, Redwood will run a hosted bench for the shortlisted models, and then we iterate.
[00:11:05] Ethan: For the pilot steps: 1) You share sample payloads and target SLOs. 2) We configure a hosted bench run and return latency/cost/quality artifacts. 3) We meet to review results and decide Dedicated vs Private. I'll add a short lab-run by next week and share logs.

[00:11:20] Priya: Timeline-wise — we want pilot results before our Q4 roadmap review. So end of September would be ideal.
[00:11:27] Marta: We can hit that. I'll send the bench template today and set expectations.

[00:11:32] Daniel: Small question — if we need on-prem later, how disruptive is migration?
[00:11:36] Ethan: Minimal at the API level. We keep the same API and routing policies; the migration work is mostly on networking, KMS, and driver validation. The console and infra abstractions remain consistent.

[00:11:47] Priya: Any mention of competitor benchmarking — can Redwood run a head-to-head vs our current vendor?
[00:11:52] Marta: Yes, with customer permission we can include a comparator. We'll need sample contracts for data usage if you want the vendor-specific numbers in our reports.

[00:11:59] Lena: Ok, last question — does Redwood's Optimize engine auto-suggest model switching during traffic spikes?
[00:12:05] Ethan: Optimize provides recommendations and can automate simple actions like increasing batch size or switching to a cheaper quantized model within configured safe thresholds. For automatic model switching we'd recommend a canary policy configured in Console.

[00:12:18] Priya: Great. Anything else from Redwood?
[00:12:21] Marta: No, thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the assets: catalog export, bench template link, SOC2 link, and a proposed pilot plan. Expect an email from me.
[00:12:32] Priya: Thanks, appreciate it.
[00:12:34] Daniel: Thanks, good session.
[00:12:36] Lena: Thanks!

[00:12:40] (call formalities, small outro)

[00:13:02] NOTE: Extended Q&A after main demo continued in a separate thread — Ethan ran a quick lab bench and pasted raw artifacts into the shared spreadsheet link; brief highlights were discussed. Several words in the live transcript may be mis-recognized (e.g., specific kernel names, vendor model nicknames). Refer to attachments for precise artifact names and lab logs.
